title: French Revolution
summary: Between 1789 and 1799 France moved from an absolute monarchy through a constitutional monarchy and a republic, the Terror and the Directory to the Consulate under Bonaparte, proclaiming equal rights while killing tens of thousands in the process.
card: A fiscal crisis brought the Estates-General to Versailles in May 1789, and within weeks the Third Estate had remade it as a National Assembly; the Bastille fell on 14 July and the Declaration of the Rights of Man was adopted on 26 August. War and distrust of the king led to the overthrow of the monarchy in August 1792, a republic in September and, in 1793-94, a Terror that probably cost some 40,000 lives. The Directory that followed was ended by Bonaparte's coup of 9-10 November 1799.
what:
The French Revolution is the decade from 1789 to 1799 in which the French state, its social order and its political vocabulary were rebuilt. The usual starting point is the opening of the Estates-General at Versailles on 5 May 1789, called to resolve the monarchy's financial crisis. Its members from the Third Estate declared themselves the National Assembly on 17 June and took the Tennis Court Oath on 20 June; the Parisian crowd took the Bastille on 14 July; the Assembly's August decrees ended the legal basis of feudalism on 4 August, and on 26 August it adopted the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, which proclaimed legal equality and national sovereignty.

For three years France was a constitutional monarchy under the Constitution of 1791. The king's attempted flight in 1791 and the war declared on Austria on 20 April 1792 undermined it, and after the attack on the Tuileries on 10 August 1792 the Convention met on 21 September 1792 and declared a republic. Louis XVI was guillotined in January 1793. Defeat abroad, civil war in the Vendee and fear of conspiracy produced the Terror, formally dated from September 1793 to the fall of Robespierre on 9 Thermidor Year II (27 July 1794). Official death sentences were about 17,000; once deaths in prison and executions without trial are added, a total near 40,000 is plausible, with the Vendee war claiming a much larger number. The Convention also abolished slavery in the French colonies in February 1794, a decision driven by the slave insurrection in Saint-Domingue.

After Thermidor the Convention wound down the Terror and the Constitution of 1795 created the Directory, which restored a property-based male franchise. The Directory was overthrown on 18-19 Brumaire Year VIII (9-10 November 1799) by Sieyes and Napoleon Bonaparte, who established the Consulate. Historians disagree about the Revolution's causes and character: the older social interpretation read it as a bourgeois revolution, revisionists stress politics, ideology and fiscal crisis, and there is no agreement on whether the Terror was a product of circumstances or of revolutionary ideas. The end date of 1799 is itself a convention; some scholars carry the Revolution to 1804 or later.

uncertainty.note: Start and end are conventional. 5 May 1789 (opening of the Estates-General) is the commonest start, though the Assembly of Notables (1787) and the parlements' revolt (1788) are sometimes counted. 9-10 November 1799 (coup of 18-19 Brumaire) is the commonest end; some historians extend the Revolution to the establishment of the Empire in 1804. Dates before 22 September 1792 were never recorded in the republican calendar at the time.

how: The immediate cause was a fiscal crisis: the monarchy was close to bankruptcy and, after the notables and the parlements refused reform, called the Estates-General for 1789. The first collision was over voting: the Third Estate wanted votes counted by head, not by order, and on 17 June it declared itself the National Assembly, then swore on 20 June not to disperse until France had a constitution. When the king dismissed the minister Necker on 11 July and troops gathered near Paris, crowds seized arms and took the Bastille on 14 July; peasants rose in the Great Fear, and on 4 August the Assembly abolished feudal privileges, followed by the Declaration of 26 August. The monarchy then lost credibility through the king's attempted flight and the war with Austria declared in April 1792; the rising of 10 August 1792 overthrew it, and the Convention proclaimed a republic on 21 September. Military defeat, the Vendee rising and the execution of the king in January 1793 radicalised politics; the Committee of Public Safety, the Law of Suspects (17 September 1793) and the Law of 22 Prairial (10 June 1794) built the machinery of the Terror. Robespierre's colleagues overthrew him on 9 Thermidor. The Directory (1795) was undermined by war and factional coups, and Sieyes and Bonaparte ended it with the troops-backed coup of 18-19 Brumaire.
why_it_matters: The Revolution made the claim that sovereignty belongs to the nation and that laws apply equally to all into a founding political text. The 1789 Declaration is still cited in French constitutional law, since the preamble of the 1958 Constitution refers to it and the Conseil constitutionnel treats its principles as binding. The Revolution also abolished feudal privilege, created the republican calendar and nationalised church property, and its wars spread these arrangements across Europe. Its record on rights was incomplete: the Assembly refused at first to extend equality to the enslaved, and only the Saint-Domingue insurrection forced the Convention to abolish slavery in February 1794, a decree Napoleon reversed in 1802, though Haiti won independence and the rest of the French colonies had to wait until 1848. The Terror left a lasting argument about whether revolutionary violence is the price of change or its corruption. Without the Revolution, the monarchy might have limped on through reform, there would have been no Brumaire and no Napoleonic Consulate in 1799, and the rights vocabulary used by later movements, from Haiti to Europe's 19th-century liberals, would have lacked its most famous charter. The same record shows how war and fear can turn a rights movement into a machine for killing tens of thousands of people.

beats.action: marker.pin { at: [48.8044, 2.1203], label: 'Estates-General open at Versailles' }
beats.caption: On 5 May 1789 the Estates-General meets at Versailles, called to deal with the crown's financial crisis.

beats.action: marker.pulse { at: [48.8044, 2.1203], label: 'National Assembly; Tennis Court Oath' }
beats.caption: The Third Estate declares itself the National Assembly on 17 June and swears on 20 June not to disperse until France has a constitution; the sovereignty of the monarch is now disputed.
On 14 July Parisians take the Bastille, held by 114 defenders; seven prisoners are inside. The governor is killed by the crowd.

beats.action: document.show { title: 'Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen' }
beats.caption: The Assembly ends feudal privilege on 4 August and on 26 August adopts a Declaration asserting equal rights and national sovereignty, which France's constitution still invokes.

beats.action: region.fill { region: France, label: 'war, 10 August 1792, Republic' }
beats.caption: War with Austria begins in April 1792, the monarchy is overthrown on 10 August and the Convention declares a republic on 21 September.

beats.action: marker.pulse { label: 'Execution of Louis XVI, Paris' }
beats.caption: Louis XVI is guillotined in January 1793, which historians such as Tackett see as the start of a killing phase of the Revolution.
From September 1793 to Thermidor Year II, about 17,000 death sentences are passed and a total near 40,000 deaths is likely, on top of the far larger toll of the Vendee war.

beats.action: flow.arcs { from: 'Paris (Convention)', to: 'French Caribbean colonies', label: 'decree abolishing slavery', weight: schematic }
beats.caption: Pressed by the Saint-Domingue insurrection, the Convention abolishes slavery in the colonies on 4 February 1794; Napoleon will restore it in 1802.

beats.action: marker.pulse { at: [48.8531, 2.3692], label: '9 Thermidor Year II' }
beats.caption: On 9 Thermidor Year II (27 July 1794) colleagues overthrow Robespierre; he is guillotined the next day and the Terror is wound down.
On 18-19 Brumaire Year VIII (9-10 November 1799) Sieyes and Bonaparte end the Directory, and Bonaparte becomes the leading consul of the new Consulate.

perspectives.holder: Classical or Marxist-influenced social interpretation (Lefebvre, Soboul and followers)
perspectives.account: Read the Revolution as a bourgeois revolution that overthrew a feudal order, and the Terror as a response to national emergency. Furet criticised this school as neo-Jacobin and economically determinist.

Cobban disputed that the bourgeoisie was a single class with revolutionary aims; Furet shifted attention to political language and ideology and saw the Terror as bound up with revolutionary ideas rather than only circumstances.

perspectives.holder: State- and war-centred accounts (Skocpol and Kestnbaum); Linton
perspectives.account: Skocpol and Kestnbaum stress geopolitical pressure and war as drivers of mobilisation and state-building; Linton stresses that the Revolution was begun by elites in a fiscal crisis, and that the 'system of terror' was ad hoc and contested.

Dates a 'killing Terror' from the king's execution in January 1793 and explains the shift by changing mentalities among revolutionaries, rejecting both the view that the Terror was the whole Revolution and the view that it was merely circumstantial.

perspectives.holder: Contemporary British ambassador (1789) versus later accounts of the Bastille
perspectives.account: A confidential report held in The National Archives put the deaths at the Bastille at seven or eight; later syntheses give 82 attackers killed and 15 more dead of wounds. Both figures are recorded as claims.

numbers.label: Death sentences passed by revolutionary courts in France, c. 1793-1794
numbers.note: 16,594 is the figure given by World History Encyclopedia (of which 2,625 in Paris; Linton gives 2,639); Tackett, via Jacobson, rounds to about 17,000. Neither source opened here names its table; the figure is traditionally linked to Donald Greer's 1935 study, which could not be opened.

numbers.label: Total deaths of the Terror including executions without trial and deaths in prison, excluding the Vendee war
numbers.note: World History Encyclopedia gives 30,000-50,000; Linton 40,000-50,000; Tackett (via Jacobson) judges about 40,000 'not unlikely'. About 10,000 are said to have died in prison (World History Encyclopedia).

numbers.label: Deaths in the Vendee war, mostly peasants and republican soldiers
numbers.note: Single-point estimate given by Linton; other estimates are far lower and far higher, and sources opened here do not agree on a range. Treat as order of magnitude only.

numbers.label: Defenders of the Bastille on 14 July 1789
numbers.note: 82 invalides and 32 Swiss reinforcements; seven prisoners held.

numbers.label: Attackers killed at the Bastille
numbers.note: World History Encyclopedia: 82 killed plus 15 who later died of wounds (total 97). The British ambassador's contemporary report put deaths at seven or eight (src-natarchives-ambassador); the low bound records that claim.

audience_note: Describes mass political killing, including executions by guillotine, drownings and deaths in prison, and the killing of the Bastille's governor by a crowd. Images included show an execution scene and a 1789 assault.

importance.justification: It ended absolute monarchy in France, issued the founding rights charter of modern republican politics, set off wars across Europe and led to the Napoleonic regime.

reviewer_note: Least sure of the Terror and Vendee death figures: Greer's 1935 tables could not be opened, so 16,594 and the 30,000-50,000 range rest on secondary summaries; the Vendee figure is a single sourced estimate.
